q.t: Which bird builds a woven hanging nest out of grass?
q.e: The male baya weaver threads grass over and under.

q.t: Hand-weaving is done on an instrument called a…
q.e: Cloth from a hand loom is called handloom fabric.

q.t: A charkha is used for…
q.e: It twists fibres into thread, faster than fingers.

q.t: Pashmina comes from…
q.e: Wool from the Changthangi goat of Ladakh.

q.t: Kanjeevaram sarees come from…
q.e: Kanjeevaram is a Tamil Nadu silk tradition.

q.t: Silk is made by…
q.e: The caterpillar spins a cocoon of one long silk thread.

q.t: Phulkari embroidery is from…
q.e: Phulkari is Punjab's famous embroidery.

q.t: Chikankari is from…
q.e: Chikan embroidery comes from Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh.

q.t: Which bird sews its nest with a leaf?
q.e: It pokes holes in a leaf edge and pulls fibre through.

q.t: Which fibre is natural?
q.e: Cotton grows on a plant; the others are synthetic.

q.t: Why does a woven mat hold together but stacked strips slide apart?
o: Each woven strip is trapped by the strips around it
q.e: Every thread both grips and is gripped.

q.t: In weaving, each row must be…
o: The opposite of the row above
The same as the row above
q.e: If two rows matched, nothing would be trapped.

q.t: Why does twisting cotton make it strong?
o: It presses short fibres together so they can't slide
q.e: Friction between tightly pressed fibres holds the thread together.

q.t: Why doesn't silk need spinning like cotton?
o: It comes as one long continuous strand
q.e: The cocoon is wound from a single strand, hundreds of metres long.

q.t: Why is silk so shiny?
o: It is smooth with no short fibre-ends to scatter light
q.e: A smooth surface reflects light evenly.

q.t: A problem with most synthetic fibres:
o: They don't rot, so stay as waste for long
q.e: Synthetic waste can last for decades.

q.t: Indian muslin was called 'woven air' because…
o: It was so fine a saree passed through a ring
q.e: Its fineness amazed the world.

q.t: Why did Gandhiji make spinning a symbol of freedom?
o: Making your own cloth meant not depending on others
q.e: That is what atmanirbhar — self-reliant — means.

q.t: Bandhani is made by…
o: Tying small parts of cloth before dyeing
q.e: Tied spots resist the dye and become dots.

q.t: Handloom uses no…
q.e: That makes it eco-friendly and possible anywhere.

q.t: A running stitch is cut in one place. What happens?
o: The seam can pull out in both directions
q.e: One thread does the whole job — like a chain failing at one link.

q.t: A woven cloth with one broken thread…
o: Still holds — just a small flaw
q.e: Thousands of threads each held by neighbours — like a net.

q.t: Why are seams knotted at both ends?
o: So the thread can't pull out
q.e: Knots stop a single-thread seam from unravelling.

q.t: Which question should we ask when choosing a fibre?
o: Which suits this job, and what happens to it afterwards?
q.e: Neither natural nor synthetic is simply better.

q.t: Why is a nylon rope better than cotton for a boat?
q.e: Synthetic fibres can be chosen for strength and water resistance.

q.t: Why is cotton comfortable in hot weather?
q.e: Cotton lets air and sweat move, keeping you cool.

q.t: Kantha began as…
o: Stitching worn-out cloths into a quilt
q.e: Its beauty grew out of thrift.

q.t: Why did each region develop its own embroidery?
o: Local cloth, threads, dyes and images were different
q.e: An embroidery is a record of a place — like the drums in Chapter 5.

q.t: Why must a weaving pattern be kept alive by weavers?
o: If the last weaver stops, the pattern is gone
q.e: Many traditions exist only in the hands of their weavers.

q.t: A Patola saree from Patan can take…
q.e: It's extremely detailed handwork.

q.t: A rope of any length can be made from fibres a few centimetres long because…
o: Twist keeps fibres pressed and gripping
q.e: Thread is thousands of short fibres held by friction.

q.t: Why is passing on an old shirt more than a small kindness?
o: All the land, water and work in it isn't wasted
q.e: Everything spent making it is still in it — only its size is used up.

q.t: A life cycle is…
o: The pattern of being born, growing, reproducing and dying
q.e: Every living thing has one; they differ in the stages.

q.t: Which statement about the baya weaver is true?
o: Young birds' first nests are rough — weaving must be learnt
q.e: Even weaving improves with practice.

q.t: How many people does handloom employ in India?
q.e: One of the largest cottage industries in the world.

q.t: Mill cloth and handloom: which is true?
o: Both exist; they are good at different things
q.e: Mills are fast and cheap; handloom keeps traditions and uses no electricity.

q.t: Which country first cultivated cotton and made cloth from it?
q.e: India's cotton changed textiles worldwide.

q.t: How could you guess a cloth is silk or a synthetic rather than cotton?
o: It looks shiny and feels smooth
q.e: Smooth fibres reflect light evenly; cotton and wool scatter it.

q.t: Ikat weaving is from…
q.e: Ikat is made in Odisha and Gujarat.

q.t: Why is synthetic cloth waste a stronger reason to reuse clothes?
o: It doesn't rot and stays as waste for decades
q.e: Throwing it away creates long-lasting waste.
